published_title: THE LITTLE GOD OF UNKEPT PROMISES

story.title: THE LITTLE GOD OF UNKEPT PROMISES
story.deck: By sunset, Mount Vey will collapse onto a city where a minor god has made every promise physically binding. Illuminara must free a father from his doorway, two children from forever, and exhausted workers from a mayor’s vow—without teaching the powerful that accountability is only for other people.
story.shape: Five scenes move from visible private bonds and a hard quarry clock, through Sef’s history of elite impunity and a worker-led design for recourse, into a costly public covenant tested during a ninety-three-second collapse. Sef freely releases literal control when accountability survives refusal; the mountain covenant holds, the trapped escape, and a renewable court gives both promises and freedom an answer.

scenes.title: The Doorway
paragraphs: *Veyra, the east ward · 08:12, ten hours before sunset*

Oren Vale leaned into his own open doorway until the tendons stood in his neck. His left boot crossed the sill. His right would not lift. Nothing visible held it, yet the floorboards groaned as if a cart horse pulled the other way.

**Lio**  
Dad, stop. Your ankle is bleeding.
His daughter knelt on the street side with a quarry alarm bell in one hand. Beyond her, a pale line of dust hung above Mount Vey. Each time the bell sounded, the mountain answered a heartbeat later.

**Oren**  
I promised your mother I would never leave you alone in this house.

**Lio**  
I am standing outside it. I am asking you to leave with me.

**Oren**  
The promise does not know the difference.

Across the lane, Mina and Cal moved with their wrists held a handspan apart by a thread of amber light. At nine they had sworn to be friends forever. At twelve, Mina had earned a place on a river school; Cal had refused to let her board the coach because every step away burned both their arms.

**Mina**  
We meant it when we said it.

**Cal**  
That is the worst part.

Illuminara came down without thunder. She put one palm against Oren’s lintel. The pressure was not in the wood. It ran under the street, through thousands of doorstones, marriage rings, guild marks and burial tablets, all converging on the black quarry above the city.

A small figure sat on the lintel where her hand had been. He was no taller than Lio’s forearm. His coat was stitched from torn contracts; his eyes were two drops of sealing wax. When he spoke, every promise in the street tightened.

**Sef**  
If words may be escaped whenever they hurt, the weak are the only ones who must believe them.

**Illuminara**  
I did not come to teach you that words are cheap.

**Sef**  
You came because the mayor’s quarry is breaking my oldest covenant. Powerful people always discover mercy when consequence reaches their own door.
The second alarm sounded. Dust rolled from Mount Vey in a thicker ribbon. Lio unfolded a quarry map. A red crack had reached the ventilation stair where three hundred night workers were still below.

**Lio**  
Forewoman Sen says the east shelf will fall at 17:42. The mayor promised work to every household. Sef made the promise true. Half the city is too exhausted to shore the shelf, and no one assigned to the quarry can leave.

**Illuminara**  
My aim is to get every person out before the shelf falls, without breaking the covenant that keeps the mountain off the city.

**Sef**  
Then begin with the part you dislike. Ask who paid when promises were only admired.
He stepped into a crack in the lintel and vanished. Oren’s right foot remained fixed.
Illuminara lifted Lio’s alarm bell and felt its chipped bronze warm in her hand. *He had not refused help. He had refused another exception made by someone strong enough to call it mercy.*

**Illuminara**  
Show me the Hall of Oaths. Then we go to the quarry together.

Lio glanced at her father. Oren stopped pulling at the threshold, wrapped his ankle, and nodded. It was not rescue yet. It was the first time that morning someone had asked him to act rather than endure.

scenes.title: What Sef Heard
paragraphs: *Hall of Oaths · 10:05, seven hours and thirty-seven minutes before collapse*

The hall had no statues. Its walls were built from promise stones: one for every vow on which another person’s safety had depended. Bright stones marked fulfilled obligations. Dark ones marked breaches. Most of the dark stones bore the crests of old councils, mining houses and temples.

Sef stood on the clerk’s table. Around him gathered Oren, Lio, Mina, Cal, Forewoman Ilya Sen, Mayor Teren Vos and forty citizens chosen by the quarry crews. No guard stood at the doors. Sef had made every official who promised public service unable to leave.

**Mayor Vos**  
Release the workers and I will sign any amendment you draft.

**Sef**  
You signed six safety amendments. When production fell, you called each one aspirational.

**Mayor Vos**  
The city would have starved.

**Ilya**  
You promised every family wages, then counted compulsory double shifts as employment. We did not starve. We broke.

Illuminara touched a dark stone bearing the mayoral crest. It held not words but consequences: Ilya’s crushed fingers; a widow’s unanswered petition; children carrying meals to parents who slept beside the lifts.

**Illuminara**  
Sef, when did you begin binding every promise literally?

**Sef**  
After the seventh council swore to repair the west retaining wall and used the money for a triumph gate. The slide killed four hundred and twelve. Their last breath was full of official language.

**Illuminara**  
So your goal is not obedience. It is recourse.
The wax in Sef’s eyes trembled, but his voice stayed hard.

**Sef**  
Recourse that cannot be postponed by the eloquent. A promise that changes when the promiser suffers is merely a weapon with a velvet handle.

**Lio**  
And a promise that cannot hear the person it was made to becomes a cage. My mother asked Dad to keep me safe, not to die inside our doorway.

**Oren**  
I used her last words because deciding what came next frightened me. Sef did not invent that.
Cal raised his glowing wrist. Mina raised hers beside it.

**Cal**  
I wanted forever because everyone in my house leaves.

**Mina**  
I stayed because his fear hurt me less than hurting him. That does not make staying freely chosen.
For one moment the amber thread slackened, then tightened again. Sef had listened; he had not conceded.

**Sef**  
If I accept intention over words, Mayor Vos will discover that he intended justice all along.

**Illuminara**  
Then do not let the promiser decide. Let the person who relied on the promise name the harm. Let release require truth, repair and a new choice—not cleverer wording.

**Mayor Vos**  
A tribunal during a mountain emergency?

**Ilya**  
A tribunal is what you call it when workers get a chair.
The hall shuddered. A line of dust fell from the ceiling. On the quarry map, the red crack crossed another support gallery. The clock now read seven hours, twenty-nine minutes.

**Sef**  
Words again. Test them where stone can answer.

He struck the table. Three promise stones rose: the mayor’s employment vow, Oren’s doorway vow, and the children’s forever vow. Beneath them lay a fourth, older and brighter than all the rest: the city’s covenant to keep the drainage channels clear so Mount Vey would sleep.

**Sef**  
Break every bond and the old covenant breaks with them. Keep every bond and the exhausted crews die. Show me accountability that survives freedom.

Illuminara did not reach for power. She asked Ilya for the quarry ledgers, Lio for the petitions no clerk had answered, and Sef for the names of those who had relied on each promise. Sef gave her the names.

scenes.title: The Price Named by the Harmed
paragraphs: *East quarry assembly floor · 13:48, three hours and fifty-four minutes before collapse*

The quarry floor had been cleared beneath a roof of cracked slate. Every eight minutes, a brass plumb bob swung farther east. Ilya had painted three evacuation lines on the ground. The workers stood behind the lines by crew, not by rank.

Illuminara could have carried them out. The covenant ran through the drainage tunnels, however, and a forced severing would send the saturated upper slope into Veyra. Her strength could hold one shelf for ninety-three seconds. The mountain held six.

**Illuminara**  
Here is the proposal. Every safety promise names its beneficiaries, duration, proof and a way to demand repair. Changed circumstances may reopen terms, but only those who relied on the promise can accept the repair. No one is bound by a promise made about them without consent.

**Sef**  
A mayor can purchase forgiveness with public money.

**Ilya**  
Not this time.

She laid three demands on the stone table. The quarry would close until an elected crew inspected every gallery. Vos would surrender the mayoral house and his family’s quarry shares to a restitution trust. For five years, half the council seats overseeing public works would belong to workers and bereaved families.

**Mayor Vos**  
My children live in that house.

**Ilya**  
Mine sleep in shifts because I have not had a full night home in eleven months.

**Mayor Vos**  
Take the shares. The house is not mine alone to give.

**Lio**  
Then ask your family. A covenant cannot begin by stealing from people who were not in the room.

Vos sent a runner. While they waited, Mina and Cal wrote their own repair: each would tell the other one thing the vow had cost; neither would ask for contact for thirty days; after that, friendship could be renewed only by two yeses.

**Cal**  
If she says no after thirty days, what holds me?

**Sef**  
Nothing.

**Cal**  
That feels like falling.

**Mina**  
I will sit with you until the coach comes. I will not promise what happens after.
Cal wept without hiding his face. Sef climbed down from the table and sat beside him. He did not loosen the amber thread.

**Sef**  
I was made from that fear. Every promise is a bridge over the fact that another being may leave.

**Illuminara**  
A bridge has two shores. A chain has one owner.

**Sef**  
And if the far shore burns the bridge after crossing?

**Ilya**  
Then we keep records, witnesses and restitution. We do not nail the traveler to the boards.
The runner returned with Vos’s family. His husband, Maro, read the demands once and placed the house key beside the quarry shares.

**Maro**  
We keep three rooms until winter. After that the house becomes the clinic the quarry should already have built.
Vos stared at the key. The cost had become a door he could not rhetoric his way around.

**Mayor Vos**  
Agreed. And I resign before the first inspection.

**Ilya**  
Resignation does not settle the ledger. You testify, disclose the diverted funds and work the drainage crews at their elected forewoman’s direction. No ceremonial shovel.

**Mayor Vos**  
Agreed.

Illuminara placed her own name on the slate. She promised to hold the east shelf for no more than ninety-three seconds when Ilya called, to obey the evacuation plan, and to submit any use of force in Veyra that day to the same public review. She offered no forever.

**Sef**  
You could leave before judgment.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. That is why the covenant records what people may do if I do: publish my breach, refuse my aid, and summon witnesses beyond this city. Trust is not certainty. It is power arranged so betrayal has an answer.
Sef looked toward the mountain. The plumb bob struck its warning mark two hours early.

**Ilya**  
The crack accelerated. New collapse time: 17:19.
No one asked Sef to believe a definition. They carried the proposal to the failing galleries for a test.

scenes.title: Ninety-Three Seconds
paragraphs: *Mount Vey, east shelf · 17:16, three minutes before collapse*

Rainwater hissed through the upper fracture. Below it, six crews moved along routes they had chosen. Ilya held the release lever that would empty the ore tram and free the north stair. Lio stood at the signal bell. Oren waited at the city doorway, still bound, ready to cross if Sef released him.

**Ilya**  
Test condition one: the workers may refuse the mayor’s employment promise without losing their claim to wages.

**Sef**  
If I release them, who keeps the drainage covenant?
Thirty-two workers raised their hands. Not one was compelled.

**Workers**  
We renew the drainage covenant for this evacuation and for thirty days. After that, renewal requires inspection, pay and a recorded vote.

**Ilya**  
Test condition two: those harmed retain the power to reject repair.

**Mina**  
I accept thirty days apart.

**Cal**  
I accept that she may not return.

Sef opened one small hand. The amber thread between the children dissolved into warm sparks. Cal staggered, then stood without grabbing Mina. Mina took his hand for three breaths and let go. Both choices held.

In the city, Oren’s right foot lifted. He crossed the doorway and ran toward the lower drainage gate with Lio’s spare key. His promise did not vanish; it changed into a record of care, harm and consent that Lio had accepted.

**Sef**  
And the mayor?

**Mayor Vos**  
Do not release my debt. Release the workers from my command.
The promise stones around the quarry flared. The ore tram gates opened. Workers who had been physically unable to abandon assigned stations moved toward the stairs.
At 17:18:07 the east shelf split.

**Ilya**  
Now, Illuminara.

Illuminara went beneath the falling shelf and raised both hands. Two million tonnes of slate stopped a spear’s length above her. The impact drove her knees into stone. The clock on Lio’s board began at ninety-three.

Sef saw the sixth crew still trapped behind a contract-marked gate. Releasing them would weaken the old covenant for eleven seconds before their voluntary renewal reached the promise stones. In those seconds the drainage channels might shear.

**Sef**  
If I keep them, the mountain sleeps and they die. If I free them, the city may fall.

**Illuminara**  
Yes.

**Sef**  
You have no better word?

**Illuminara**  
Only this: I will hold what I can. They must choose what they will carry. You must choose what you were made to protect.
The clock passed fifty-eight. A support cracked against Illuminara’s shoulder. She did not command Sef or promise that no one would be hurt.
Sef looked at Ilya, not at the mayor.

**Sef**  
If I open the gate, will your crew renew the drainage covenant before they reach the north stair?

**Ilya**  
Ask them.

Through the bars, the sixth crew answered one by one. Twenty-one said yes. Three said no; they had been on duty thirty-six hours and would accept no new promise until they slept. Ilya assigned their section to rested volunteers, who consented on the record.
At seventy-two seconds, Sef opened the gate.

For eleven seconds, Mount Vey moved. Oren reached the lower gate and opened the emergency spillway. Lio struck the bell in the new sequence designed by the crews. Volunteers renewed only the drainage work they had named. The bright covenant stone held.
At eighty-eight seconds, the last worker crossed the north stair. Ilya dropped the ore tram into the empty cut, where its weight pulled the fractured shelf away from the city.

**Ilya**  
Clear!

Illuminara released the stone at ninety-two seconds. The shelf fell into the abandoned quarry. The old processing hall, three cranes and the mayoral triumph arch disappeared under dust. No house in Veyra moved.

For a moment Mina laughed—not because the loss was small, but because Cal had let her run and had run beside someone else. Illuminara laughed too, breathless and astonished. The sound was her own, not a lesson for anyone.
Sef stood on her dust-covered shoulder. He was still small. He no longer looked like a jailer, but neither did he look harmless.

**Sef**  
Three refused, and the covenant lived.

**Illuminara**  
Accountability survived freedom.

**Sef**  
Once is evidence, not faith.

**Ilya**  
Good. Come inspect the next renewal.

scenes.title: The Court of Open Hands
paragraphs: *Veyra, the former mayoral house · dawn, the following day*

The front rooms had become a temporary clinic before the dust settled. Maro and his children occupied three rooms upstairs under the winter term they had negotiated. The quarry shares were sealed in the restitution trust. Vos slept on a bench outside the records office, waiting to testify.
At the long table sat workers, bereaved families, apprentices, clerks and two seats kept empty for people who had not yet decided whether to join. Above them hung no image of Sef.
Sef sat in one of the empty seats.

**Clerk Ana**  
The Court of Open Hands has three powers: preserve the record, hear those who relied on a promise, and certify repair or release. It cannot compel a new promise.

**Sef**  
And my power?

**Ilya**  
You may make concealed consequences visible. You may not bind a body until the person harmed has been heard and immediate safety requires it. Every binding expires unless this court renews it with the affected people’s consent.

**Sef**  
You offer a god a clerkship.

**Lio**  
We offer you witnesses who cannot be dismissed as a superstition when officials break their word.
Sef studied the dark stones carried from the old hall. They were no longer hidden in walls. Each lay beside a petition and the name of someone empowered to answer it.

**Sef**  
I will serve for thirty days. Then I choose again.

**Ilya**  
So do we.
Oren entered through the front door carrying a kettle. He paused on the sill by habit, then crossed. Lio did not applaud. She took the heavier handle, and together they brought tea to the night crew.

**Oren**  
I cannot repair twelve years by crossing once.

**Lio**  
No. But today you crossed when I needed you outside.

Mina’s river coach left at noon. Cal came to the platform with Sef and did not ask for a promise. Mina gave Cal a paper address that might change. Cal gave her a carved whistle and told her she did not have to use it.

At Mount Vey, rested volunteers cleared the drainage channels under Ilya’s plan. The quarry stayed closed. Wages came from the seized shares. Three families rejected the first restitution offers, and the court recorded the refusals without punishing them.

Vos disclosed the diverted funds and named the councilors who had approved them. When he tried to explain that every choice had protected employment, Ilya made him read the night-shift injury list before he continued.

Illuminara submitted her ninety-two seconds of force to review. A rigger objected that the falling shelf had shattered a memorial crane. She listened, helped recover its nameplate, and accepted the court’s requirement that it be rebuilt before any monument to the rescue.
Sef watched all of this with the severe attention of a creature learning that consequence could have more than one shape.

**Sef**  
The weak still need words they can trust.

**Illuminara**  
Yes.

**Sef**  
Freedom will still be used as an excuse by the strong.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. That is why freedom without recourse is unfinished.

**Sef**  
And recourse without freedom becomes me.

He did not apologize for the bindings. Some people were not ready to forgive him, and the court did not ask them to. He placed his sealing-wax hand on the first thirty-day covenant beside Ilya’s inked thumbprint.

The promise stones warmed one by one beneath the city. Mount Vey settled, not because every word had become unbreakable, but because enough people had freely taken responsibility for the water, the wages and one another—and because those who might be harmed now had a place from which to answer.
Illuminara left Veyra by the east road after breakfast. Behind her, Sef rang Lio’s chipped bell for the next hearing. Two empty chairs remained at the table. No one filled them by force.

Illuminara looked down at the clause she had thought was fair. *Sef knew not only how promises trapped people, but how power escaped them.* She struck the sentence through.

Better. Not safe. Better.

I am not. Maro and the children own half. I will not promise away what is theirs, even now.

Then for once ask the people whose life your promise would spend.

No. The children do not lose their home because Teren lied at work. The clinic may use the ground floor today. We keep three rooms through winter. In spring, the trust may buy our half at an assessed price; Teren’s half and every quarry share pass to it now.

**Ilya**  
The clinic opens today, the trust cannot evict you before spring, and his restitution cannot pay you for his own half. I accept that.

Vos looked at the key Maro had refused to surrender. The compromise cost him more than a theatrical forfeiture: his family kept a boundary he could not control, while his own title, office and shares were gone.

**Mayor Vos**  
I disclose the diverted funds and work the drainage crews under their elected forewoman. No ceremonial shovel.

**Ilya**  
That settles the first line, not the ledger.

Illuminara placed her own name on the slate. She promised to hold the east shelf for no more than ninety-three seconds when Ilya called, to obey the evacuation plan, and to submit any use of force in Veyra that day to the same public review. She offered no forever.

**Sef**  
You could leave before judgment.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. The record gives people an answer if I do: publish my breach, refuse my aid and summon witnesses beyond this city. Trust is not certainty. It is power arranged so betrayal has an answer.

Sef looked toward the lower terraces, where Lio’s runners were already carrying the names he had supplied in the Hall. The people protected by the drainage covenant would be asked what risk, if any, they would accept.
The plumb bob struck its warning mark two hours early.

**Ilya**

No one asked Sef to believe a definition. They carried a corrected proposal, an unclaimed witness seal and three possible evacuation answers to the failing galleries.

scenes.title: Ninety-Three Seconds
paragraphs: *Mount Vey, east shelf · 17:16, three minutes before collapse*

Rainwater hissed through the upper fracture. Below it, six crews moved along routes they had chosen. Ilya held the release lever that would empty the ore tram and free the north stair. Lio stood at the signal bell. Oren waited at the city doorway, still bound, ready to cross if Sef released him.

At the lower spillway stood Ressa Daan, whose bakery and cellar occupied the first terrace, and Toma Ely, chosen by the east-lane households. They held the reply bells. No one claimed they spoke for the whole city; they carried the recorded answers of the people on the routes that would take the eleven-second surge.

**Ilya**  
Test condition one: the workers may refuse the mayor’s employment promise without losing their claim to wages.

**Sef**  
If I release them, who keeps the drainage covenant?
Thirty-two workers raised their hands. Not one was compelled.

**Workers**  
We renew the drainage covenant for this evacuation and for thirty days. After that, renewal requires inspection, pay and a recorded vote.

**Ilya**  
Test condition two: those harmed retain the power to reject repair.

**Mina**  
I accept thirty days apart.

**Cal**  
I accept that she may not return.

Sef opened one small hand. The amber thread between the children dissolved into warm sparks. Cal staggered, then stood without grabbing Mina. Mina took his hand for three breaths and let go. Both choices held.

In the city, Oren’s right foot lifted. He crossed the doorway and ran toward the lower drainage gate with Lio’s spare key. His promise did not vanish; it changed into a record of care, harm and consent that Lio had accepted.

**Sef**  
And the mayor?

**Mayor Vos**  
Do not release my debt. Release the workers from my command.
The promise stones around the quarry flared. The ore tram gates opened. Workers who had been physically unable to abandon assigned stations moved toward the stairs.
At 17:18:07 the east shelf split.

**Ilya**  
Now, Illuminara.

Illuminara went beneath the falling shelf and raised both hands. Two million tonnes of slate stopped a spear’s length above her. The impact drove her knees into stone. The clock on Lio’s board began at ninety-three.

Sef saw the sixth crew still trapped behind a contract-marked gate. Releasing them would weaken the old covenant for eleven seconds before the volunteers’ renewal reached the promise stones. In those seconds the lower spillway would flood and the east retaining road might go.

**Sef**  
If I keep them, the mountain sleeps and they die. If I free them, other people pay.

**Illuminara**  
Then ask the people who would pay.
Lio rang the question sequence: eleven seconds, lower spillway, east road. Ressa’s bell answered once: yes with a condition. Toma’s answered twice: no.

**Ressa**  
Keep the spillway open even if my cellar floods. My ovens are not worth a crew.

**Toma**  
The east lane is not clear. Six households are still moving the bedbound. No gate until Lio gives three bells.

The clock passed forty-one. Ilya changed the plan. The north-stair crew abandoned two carts of shoring timber and ran to carry the last east-lane residents above the red line. The lost timber meant the processing hall could not be saved.

**Sef**  
You accept the cellar and the road?

**Ressa**  
I accept my cellar. Toma speaks for the road only when his people are clear.
The clock passed fifty-eight. A support cracked against Illuminara’s shoulder. She did not command Sef or promise that no one would be hurt.
At sixty-four seconds, Lio heard three reply bells from the east lane and struck three of her own. Toma answered once. The condition had been met; his no had become a yes without being overruled.
Sef looked at Ilya, not at the mayor.

**Sef**  
If I open the gate, will your crew renew the drainage covenant before they reach the north stair?

**Ilya**  
Ask them.

Through the bars, the sixth crew answered one by one. Twenty-one said yes. Three said no; they had been on duty thirty-six hours and would accept no new promise until they slept. Ilya assigned their section to rested volunteers, who consented on the record.

At seventy-two seconds, Sef glanced at the plain iron witness seal Lio had left beside the lever. He could have opened the gate without it, and the offer had not been made as payment. He picked up only the witness key.

**Sef**  
One hearing. Then I choose again.
At seventy-five seconds, Sef opened the gate.

For eleven seconds, Mount Vey moved. Oren reached the lower gate and locked the emergency spillway open. Brown water filled Ressa’s cellar and tore the east retaining road into the abandoned orchard. The six households were already above it. Lio struck the new sequence; rested volunteers renewed only the drainage work they had named. The bright covenant stone held.
At eighty-eight seconds, the last worker crossed the north stair. Ilya dropped the ore tram into the empty cut, where its weight pulled the fractured shelf away from the city.

**Ilya**  
Clear!

Illuminara released the stone at ninety-two seconds. The shelf fell into the abandoned quarry. The old processing hall, three cranes and the mayoral triumph arch disappeared under dust. No house in Veyra moved.

For a moment Mina laughed—not because the loss was small, but because Cal had let her run and had run beside someone else. Illuminara laughed too, breathless and astonished. The sound was her own, not a lesson for anyone.
Sef stood on her dust-covered shoulder with the witness key closed in his wax hand. He was still small. He no longer looked like a jailer, but neither did he look harmless.

**Sef**  
Three workers refused. Toma refused until his people were clear. The covenant lived.

**Illuminara**  
Accountability survived freedom, and freedom changed the plan.

**Sef**  
Once is evidence, not faith.

**Ilya**  
Good. Come witness the cost before the next renewal.

scenes.title: The Court of Open Hands
paragraphs: *Veyra, the former mayoral house · dawn, the following day*

The front rooms had become a temporary clinic before the dust settled. Maro and his children occupied three rooms upstairs under the winter term they had negotiated. The quarry shares were sealed in the restitution trust. Vos slept on a bench outside the records office, waiting to testify.
At the long table sat workers, bereaved families, apprentices, clerks and two seats kept empty for people who had not yet decided whether to join. Above them hung no image of Sef.
Sef sat in one of the empty seats and set the witness key beside his hand. The chair was the continuation of an offer he had accepted for one hearing, not a reward for opening the gate.

**Ilya**  
This court preserves the record, hears the people who relied on a promise, and certifies repair or release. It cannot compel a new promise.

**Sef**  
And my power?

**Ilya**  
You may make concealed consequences visible. You may not bind a body until the person harmed has been heard and immediate safety requires it. Every binding expires unless this court renews it with the affected people’s consent.

**Sef**  
You offer a god a clerkship.

**Lio**  
We offer you witnesses who cannot be dismissed as a superstition when officials break their word.
Sef studied the dark stones carried from the old hall. They were no longer hidden in walls. Each lay beside a petition and the name of someone empowered to answer it.

**Sef**  
I will serve for thirty days. Then I choose again.

**Ilya**  
So do we.
Oren entered through the front door carrying a kettle. He paused on the sill by habit, then crossed. Lio did not applaud. She took the heavier handle, and together they brought tea to the night crew.

**Oren**  
I cannot repair twelve years by crossing once.

**Lio**  
No. But today you crossed when I needed you outside.

Mina’s river coach left at noon. Cal came to the platform with Sef and did not ask for a promise. Mina gave Cal a paper address that might change. Cal gave her a carved whistle and told her she did not have to use it.

At Mount Vey, rested volunteers cleared the drainage channels under Ilya’s plan. The quarry stayed closed. Wages came from the seized shares. Ressa’s bakery worked from the clinic kitchen while the city repaid the flooded cellar; the east road remained broken through winter. Three families rejected the first restitution offers, and the court recorded the refusals without punishing them.

Vos disclosed the diverted funds and named the councilors who had approved them. When he tried to explain that every choice had protected employment, Ilya made him read the night-shift injury list before he continued.

Illuminara submitted her ninety-two seconds of force to review. A rigger objected that the falling shelf had shattered a memorial crane. She listened, helped recover its nameplate, and accepted the court’s requirement that it be rebuilt before any monument to the rescue.
Sef watched all of this with the severe attention of a creature learning that consequence could have more than one shape.

**Sef**  
The weak still need words they can trust.

**Illuminara**  
Yes.

**Sef**  
Freedom will still be used as an excuse by the strong.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. That is why freedom without recourse is unfinished.

**Sef**  
And recourse without freedom becomes me.

He did not apologize for the bindings. Some people were not ready to forgive him, and the court did not ask them to. He placed his sealing-wax hand on the first thirty-day covenant beside Ilya’s inked thumbprint.

The promise stones warmed one by one beneath the city. Mount Vey settled, not because every word had become unbreakable, but because enough people had freely taken responsibility for the water, the wages and one another—and because those who might be harmed now had a place from which to answer.
Illuminara left Veyra by the east road after breakfast. Behind her, Sef rang Lio’s chipped bell for the next hearing. Two empty chairs remained at the table. No one filled them by force.

story.title: THE LITTLE GOD OF UNKEPT PROMISES
story.deck: By sunset, Mount Vey will collapse onto a city where a minor god has made every promise physically binding. Illuminara must free a father from his doorway, two children from forever, and exhausted workers from a mayor’s vow—without teaching the powerful that accountability is only for other people.
story.shape: Five scenes move from visible private bonds and a hard quarry clock, through Sef’s history of elite impunity and his discovery of a loophole in Illuminara’s first design, into a worker-built rescue whose ninety-three-second tram sequence and consent conditions are visible before they are tested. A flooded cellar and lost road make the eleven-second risk real. Offered a terminable witness key before the crisis, Sef freely releases literal control; the trapped escape and a renewable court gives both promises and freedom an answer.

scenes.title: The Doorway
paragraphs: *Veyra, the east ward · 08:12, ten hours before sunset*

Oren Vale leaned into his own open doorway until the tendons stood in his neck. His left boot crossed the sill. His right would not lift. Nothing visible held it, yet the floorboards groaned as if a cart horse pulled the other way.

**Lio**  
Dad, stop. Your ankle is bleeding.
His daughter knelt on the street side with a quarry alarm bell in one hand. Beyond her, a pale line of dust hung above Mount Vey. Each time the bell sounded, the mountain answered a heartbeat later.

**Oren**  
I promised your mother I would never leave you alone in this house.

**Lio**  
I am standing outside it. I am asking you to leave with me.

**Oren**  
The promise does not know the difference.

Across the lane, Mina and Cal moved with their wrists held a handspan apart by a thread of amber light. At nine they had sworn to be friends forever. At twelve, Mina had earned a place on a river school; Cal had refused to let her board the coach because every step away burned both their arms.

**Mina**  
We meant it when we said it.

**Cal**  
That is the worst part.

Illuminara came down without thunder. She put one palm against Oren’s lintel. The pressure was not in the wood. It ran under the street, through thousands of doorstones, marriage rings, guild marks and burial tablets, all converging on the black quarry above the city.

A small figure sat on the lintel where her hand had been. He was no taller than Lio’s forearm. His coat was stitched from torn contracts; his eyes were two drops of sealing wax. When he spoke, every promise in the street tightened.

**Sef**  
If words may be escaped whenever they hurt, the weak are the only ones who must believe them.

**Illuminara**  
I did not come to teach you that words are cheap.

**Sef**  
You came because the mayor’s quarry is breaking my oldest covenant. Powerful people always discover mercy when consequence reaches their own door.
The second alarm sounded. Dust rolled from Mount Vey in a thicker ribbon. Lio unfolded a quarry map. A red crack had reached the ventilation stair where three hundred night workers were still below.

**Lio**  
Forewoman Sen says the east shelf will fall at 17:42. The mayor promised work to every household. Sef made the promise true. Half the city is too exhausted to shore the shelf, and no one assigned to the quarry can leave.

**Illuminara**  
My aim is to get every person out before the shelf falls, without breaking the covenant that keeps the mountain off the city.

**Sef**  
Then begin with the part you dislike. Ask who paid when promises were only admired.
He stepped into a crack in the lintel and vanished. Oren’s right foot remained fixed.
Illuminara lifted Lio’s alarm bell and felt its chipped bronze warm in her hand. *He had not refused help. He had refused another exception made by someone strong enough to call it mercy.*

**Illuminara**  
Show me the Hall of Oaths. Then we go to the quarry together.

Lio glanced at her father. Oren stopped pulling at the threshold, wrapped his ankle, and nodded. It was not rescue yet. It was the first time that morning someone had asked him to act rather than endure.

scenes.title: What Sef Heard
paragraphs: *Hall of Oaths · 10:05, seven hours and thirty-seven minutes before collapse*

The hall had no statues. Its walls were built from promise stones: one for every vow on which another person’s safety had depended. Bright stones marked fulfilled obligations. Dark ones marked breaches. Most of the dark stones bore the crests of old councils, mining houses and temples.

Sef stood on the clerk’s table. Around him gathered Oren, Lio, Mina, Cal, Forewoman Ilya Sen, Mayor Teren Vos and forty citizens chosen by the quarry crews. No guard stood at the doors. Sef had made every official who promised public service unable to leave.

**Mayor Vos**  
Release the workers and I will sign any amendment you draft.

**Sef**  
You signed six safety amendments. When production fell, you called each one aspirational.

**Mayor Vos**  
The city would have starved.

**Ilya**  
You promised every family wages, then counted compulsory double shifts as employment. We did not starve. We broke.

Illuminara touched a dark stone bearing the mayoral crest. It held not words but consequences: Ilya’s crushed fingers; a widow’s unanswered petition; children carrying meals to parents who slept beside the lifts.

**Illuminara**  
Sef, when did you begin binding every promise literally?

**Sef**  
After the seventh council swore to repair the west retaining wall and used the money for a triumph gate. The slide killed four hundred and twelve. Their last breath was full of official language.

**Illuminara**  
So your goal is not obedience. It is recourse.
The wax in Sef’s eyes trembled, but his voice stayed hard.

**Sef**  
Recourse that cannot be postponed by the eloquent. A promise that changes when the promiser suffers is merely a weapon with a velvet handle.

**Lio**  
And a promise that cannot hear the person it was made to becomes a cage. My mother asked Dad to keep me safe, not to die inside our doorway.

**Oren**  
I used her last words because deciding what came next frightened me. Sef did not invent that.
Cal raised his glowing wrist. Mina raised hers beside it.

**Cal**  
I wanted forever because everyone in my house leaves.

**Mina**  
I stayed because his fear hurt me less than hurting him. That does not make staying freely chosen.
For one moment the amber thread slackened, then tightened again. Sef had listened; he had not conceded.

**Sef**  
If I accept intention over words, Mayor Vos will discover that he intended justice all along.

**Illuminara**  
Then do not let the promiser decide. Let the person who relied on the promise name the harm. Let release require truth, repair and a new choice—not cleverer wording.

**Mayor Vos**  
A tribunal during a mountain emergency?

**Ilya**  
A tribunal is what you call it when workers get a chair.
The hall shuddered. A line of dust fell from the ceiling. On the quarry map, the red crack crossed another support gallery. The clock now read seven hours, twenty-nine minutes.

**Sef**  
Words again. Test them where stone can answer.

He struck the table. Three promise stones rose: the mayor’s employment vow, Oren’s doorway vow, and the children’s forever vow. Beneath them lay a fourth, older and brighter than all the rest: the city’s covenant to keep the drainage channels clear so Mount Vey would sleep.

**Sef**  
Break every bond and the old covenant breaks with them. Keep every bond and the exhausted crews die. Show me accountability that survives freedom.

Illuminara did not reach for power. She asked Ilya for the quarry ledgers, Lio for the petitions no clerk had answered, and Sef for the names of those who had relied on each promise. Sef gave her the names.

scenes.title: The Price Named by the Harmed
paragraphs: *East quarry assembly floor · 13:48, three hours and fifty-four minutes before collapse*

The quarry floor had been cleared beneath a roof of cracked slate. Every eight minutes, a brass plumb bob swung farther east. Ilya had painted three evacuation lines on the ground. The workers stood behind the lines by crew, not by rank.

Illuminara could have carried them out. The covenant ran through the drainage tunnels, however, and a forced severing would send the saturated upper slope into Veyra. Her strength could hold one shelf for ninety-three seconds. The mountain held six.

**Illuminara**  
Here is my first proposal. Every safety promise names its beneficiaries, duration, proof and a way to demand repair. Changed circumstances may reopen its terms. Those harmed decide whether repair is enough.

**Sef**  
Who declares the circumstances changed?

**Illuminara**  
Either party could ask—

**Sef**  
Then Mayor Vos will call falling profits a changed circumstance. He will reopen the promise, keep the benefit and describe the breach as negotiation. You have built him a polite door.
Illuminara looked down at the clause she had thought was fair. *Sef knew not only how promises trapped people, but how power escaped them.* She struck the sentence through.

**Illuminara**  
Only a person who relied on the promise may trigger a reopening. Immediate danger may justify a provisional departure, but it starts a public repair hearing within one day. The promiser cannot rewrite the harm.

**Ilya**  
And the hearing begins with the injured, not the office that broke the promise.

**Sef**  
Better. Not safe. Better.

Ilya rolled the quarry cutaway across the slate. The loaded waste tram stood above the north stair on a relief rail whose haul cable crossed the east fracture. Illuminara traced the crack with two fingers and marked the point where the cable would take the load. Ilya checked the tram mass against the six crews’ recorded weights, then made the north-stair release and the counterweight one timed sequence. The workers—not a hidden machine—would set the brake, clear the route and call the final latch.

**Illuminara**  
I can hold the shelf for the tram’s ninety-three-second descent. Not for a hundred. If the route changes, you call the change.

**Ilya**  
Then your strength follows our clock.

Ilya laid three demands on the stone table. The quarry would close until an elected crew inspected every gallery. Vos would surrender his quarry shares to a restitution trust. For five years, half the council seats overseeing public works would belong to workers and bereaved families.
Vos removed the mayoral seal and signed away his office, his half of the house and every quarry share. He sent a runner for Maro and the children before anyone could mistake his signature for theirs.

While they waited, Mina and Cal wrote their own repair: each would tell the other one thing the vow had cost; neither would ask for contact for thirty days; after that, friendship could be renewed only by two yeses.

**Cal**  
If she says no after thirty days, what holds me?

**Sef**  
Nothing.

**Cal**  
That feels like falling.

**Mina**  
I will sit with you until the coach comes. I will not promise what happens after.
Cal wept without hiding his face. Sef climbed down from the table and sat beside him. He did not loosen the amber thread.

**Sef**  
I was made from that fear. Every promise is a bridge over the fact that another being may leave.

Lio placed an unused witness seal on the floor beside him. It was plain iron, cut for two keys. Her written offer gave Sef the witness key for one hearing only, or permission to leave it untouched. The quarry gate was not its price, and no one could bind him to the chair.

**Sef**  
A place offered can become another promise.

**Illuminara**  
So it expires after one hearing. You choose again. If you never take it, the chair remains empty and the court still owes you nothing.
Sef did not touch the seal. He also did not step away from it.

The runner returned with Vos’s family. Maro read the demands twice, closed his hand around the house key and refused to spend the children’s home on Teren’s debt. He conceded one concrete term: they would keep three rooms through winter while the clinic used the ground floor. The remaining purchase, trust and repair terms would be heard after the evacuation.

Vos reached for the key, stopped, and signed only the property and shares that were his to give. Ilya turned the page toward the waiting witnesses. His title was gone; his family’s boundary remained outside his control.

Illuminara signed beneath the tram calculation: ninety-three seconds when Ilya called, the evacuation route above her improvisation, and the same public review for any force she used in Veyra that day. She offered no forever.

**Sef**  
You could leave before judgment.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. The record gives people an answer if I do: publish my breach, refuse my aid and summon witnesses beyond this city. Trust is not certainty. It is power arranged so betrayal has an answer.

Sef looked toward the lower terraces, where Lio’s runners were already carrying the names he had supplied in the Hall. The people protected by the drainage covenant would be asked what risk, if any, they would accept.
The plumb bob struck its warning mark twenty-three minutes early.

Maro and his children kept three rooms upstairs through winter; in spring, the trust could offer an assessed purchase only if they accepted it. Vos’s half of the house and every quarry share he owned were sealed in the restitution trust. He slept on a bench outside the records office, waiting to testify.
At the long table sat workers, bereaved families, apprentices, clerks and two seats kept empty for people who had not yet decided whether to join. Above them hung no image of Sef.
Sef sat in one of the empty seats and set the witness key beside his hand. The chair continued an offer he had accepted for one hearing, not a reward for opening the gate.

**Ilya**  
This court preserves the record, hears the people who relied on a promise, and certifies repair or release. It cannot compel a new promise.

**Sef**  
And my power?

**Ilya**  
You may make concealed consequences visible. You may not bind a body until the person harmed has been heard and immediate safety requires it. Every binding expires unless this court renews it with the affected people’s consent.

**Sef**  
You offer a god a clerkship.

**Lio**  
We offer you witnesses who cannot be dismissed as a superstition when officials break their word.
Sef studied the dark stones carried from the old hall. They were no longer hidden in walls. Each lay beside a petition and the name of someone empowered to answer it.

**Sef**  
I will serve for thirty days. Then I choose again.

**Ilya**  
So do we.
Oren entered through the front door carrying a kettle. He paused on the sill by habit, then crossed. Lio did not applaud. She took the heavier handle, and together they brought tea to the night crew.

**Oren**  
I cannot repair twelve years by crossing once.

**Lio**  
No. But today you crossed when I needed you outside.

Mina’s river coach left at noon. Cal came to the platform with Sef and did not ask for a promise. Mina gave Cal a paper address that might change. Cal gave her a carved whistle and told her she did not have to use it.

At Mount Vey, rested volunteers cleared the drainage channels under Ilya’s plan. The quarry stayed closed and wages came from the seized shares. Ressa’s cellar remained flooded; the east road would stay broken through winter. Three families rejected the first restitution offers, and the court recorded their refusals without punishment.

Vos disclosed the diverted funds and named the councilors who had approved them. When he tried to explain that every choice had protected employment, Ilya made him read the night-shift injury list before he continued.

Illuminara submitted her ninety-two seconds of force to review. A rigger objected that the falling shelf had shattered a memorial crane. She listened, recovered its nameplate with him, and accepted the requirement that the crane be rebuilt before any monument to the rescue.
Sef watched with the severe attention of a creature learning that consequence could have more than one shape.

Before she left, Illuminara set Lio’s chipped bell within his reach and opened her palm beneath the edge of his chair. Sef looked at the offered hand, then climbed down by the chair rung instead. She withdrew without turning his refusal into a lesson and left the bell where he could choose it.

**Sef**  
The weak still need words they can trust.

**Illuminara**  
Yes.

**Sef**  
Freedom will still be used as an excuse by the strong.

**Illuminara**  
Yes. That is why freedom without recourse is unfinished.

**Sef**  
And recourse without freedom becomes me.

He did not apologize for the bindings. Some people were not ready to forgive him, and the court did not ask them to. He placed his sealing-wax hand on the first thirty-day covenant beside Ilya’s inked thumbprint.
Illuminara left Veyra by the east road after breakfast. Behind her, Sef rang Lio’s chipped bell for the next hearing. Two empty chairs remained at the table. No one filled them by force.
